Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

Splicing Factor 3b Subunit 1 (SF3B1), a core component of the spliceosome, undergoes dynamic
phosphorylation and dephosphorylation during the splicing cycle to regulate pre-mRNA splicing.
Twenty-eight threonine/proline repeats are phosphorylated by CDK11 during spliceosome
activation and remain phosphorylated in the catalytically active spliceosomes. The function of
phosphorylated SF3B1 (P-SF3B1), and the identity of spliceosomes stalled by CDK11 inhibition
remain unclear. Using quantitative proteomics of chromatin-associated spliceosomes, we identify
a previously uncharacterized intermediate complex BOTS964, arrested by CDK11 inhibitor OTS964,
that incorporates the nineteen-related (NTR) but not nineRteen (NTC) complex. iCLIP-seq revealed
that P-SF3B1 engages with the U6 snRNA internal stem-loop (ISL), suggesting a potential role in
stabilizing the RNA catalytic core. We further demonstrate that P-SF3B1 is recognized by
forkhead-associated (FHA) domain of SNIP1, which promotes recruitment of retention and
splicing (RES) complex during spliceosome activation. Acute SNIP1 depletion disrupts RES
incorporation, causes widespread splicing defects, and promotes hyperphosphorylation of SF3B1
by CDK11. Mutations in SNIP1 FHA domain, including the neurodevelopmental disorder-
associated E366G variant, impair P-SF3B1 binding, pre-mRNA splicing, and cell viability.
Together, these findings uncover the phosphorylation-dependent CDK11/P-SF3B1/SNIP1
signaling axis that is critical for pre-mRNA splicing and cellular proliferation and provide a
mechanistic insight into its dysregulation in disease.

---

## Introduction

Transcription of eukaryotic genes produces RNA precursors called pre-mRNAs, which contain
non-coding introns. Introns are removed by spliceosome in the process of pre-mRNA splicing. The
spliceosome is a dynamic RNA-protein complex that assembles on intron sequences through a
series of steps involving the sequential recruitment and release of five small nuclear
ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs): U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6, along with numerous non-snRNP
proteins. This process is accompanied by significant structural rearrangements. As a result, a series
of intermediate spliceosome complexes are formed, including ES, A, B, Bact, B*, C, C*, P, and ILS.
Pre-mRNA splicing consists of four key steps: spliceosome assembly (E→B), catalytic activation
(B→B*), two-step catalysis of splicing (B*→P), and spliceosome disassembly (P→ILS) 1-6. While
the roles of kinases and their substrates in facilitating transitions between intermediates are
essential, they remain poorly understood 7-9.

Activation of the spliceosome occurs as it transitions from the B to the Bact complex, leading to
the formation of the catalytically active U2/U6 snRNA structure. This activation progresses via
two intermediates, pre-Bact1 and pre-Bact2, and requires the release and recruitment of about 20 and
25 proteins, respectively 10-12. A key event in this activation is the unwinding of the U4/U6 snRNA
duplex, followed by the release of the U4 snRNP and B-specific proteins, and the recruitment of
various protein complexes such as the NTC (Nineteen), NTR (Nineteen-related), RES (retention
and splicing), and IBC (intron-binding) 12-16. In the activated spliceosome (Bact), the newly formed
U2/U6 snRNA catalytic center is stabilized by various proteins, including components of the NTR
and NTC complexes 12,17-19. The catalytic center remains static until the ILS complex 4. In higher
eukaryotes, this activation also requires the action of CDK11, which phosphorylates SF3B1, a core
splicing factor and component of the U2 snRNP. The inhibition of CDK11 with OTS964 traps the
spliceosome in a B-like intermediate, in which U4 snRNA and B-specific proteins remain
associated, and RES and IBC complexes unbound 8,20. The precise composition of the stalled
spliceosome however, remains unknown.

Human SF3B1 consists of an N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and a C-terminal
twenty HEAT-repeats domain 21. These regions serve distinct and essential roles in the
spliceosome lifecycle and are targeted by small molecules that disrupt spliceosome assembly and
have antiproliferative effects 8,22-26. While the functions of the HEAT-repeats are relatively well-
understood 21, the roles of the IDR, due to its structural flexibility, which prevents its visualization
in cryo-EM structures, remains largely unclear 20. The IDR acts as a dynamic interaction hub for
proteins and RNA 8,27-30, containing a cluster of 28 threonine/proline (Thr/Pro) CDK-consensus
sites that overlap with several U2AF homology ligand motifs (ULM)s 20,27,28,31,32. These motifs
serve as binding sites for splicing factors (such as U2AF65, PUF60, TAT-SF1, RBM39, and
SPF45(RBM17) when IDR is unphosphorylated in the A intermediate 31,33-36. Upon the formation
of the Bact complex, the IDR becomes fully phosphorylated, a state that persists until the second
catalytic reaction (C complex) 8,20,27, when SF3B1 is dephosphorylated by the PP1 phosphatase
37,38. RNA immunoprecipitation coupled to qPCR (RIP-qPCR) showed that phosphorylated SF3B1
(P-SF3B1) associates with U6 snRNA 8. However, it remains unclear whether this interaction is
direct and where at U6 snRNA the P-SF3B1 binds. Additionally, interacting proteins (readers) of
P-SF3B1 and their functions in the activated and catalytically active spliceosomes (B*→C) also
remain elusive.

SNIP1, a component of the trimeric RES complex (which also includes RBMX2 and BUD13) 39,40,
is integrated into the spliceosome during activation and is essential for the assembly of Bact in both
yeast and humans 12,13,40,41. The knockdown of SNIP1 and other RES subunits results in retention
of mostly short and GC-rich introns in human cells 42. A similar phenotype is observed in zebrafish
models with loss-of-function mutations in RES components 43. SNIP1 contains a conserved
forkhead-associated (FHA) domain, a putative P-Thr-binding module 44,45, with unknown
function. A recent study suggested that it is required for the interaction with RNPS1, possibly
affecting the post-transcriptional splicing of detained introns 46. A biallelic mutation (E366G) in
SNIP1, located near the FHA domain, has been associated with a complex neurodevelopmental
disorder in 35 individuals from the Amish community 47,48, although the underlying mechanistic
defect caused by the mutation is unknown. Other aberrations of SNIP1 have been linked to
neurogenesis and neurodegeneration, both in human and zebrafish 43,46,48,49. SNIP1 has also been
implicated in transcription regulation and oncogenesis 50-55, highlighting its clinical relevance.

In this study, we demonstrate that the CDK11 inhibitor OTS964 traps the spliceosome in a novel
intermediate, with the NTR complex integrated but the NTC complex not associated. We show
that P-SF3B1 localizes to U6 snRNA´s internal stem-loop (ISL), potentially contributing to the
formation and stabilization of the U2/U6 snRNA catalytic center in the activated spliceosomes.
Additionally, we identify the FHA domain of SNIP1 as a “reader” of P-SF3B1, guiding the
recruitment and assembly of the RES complex during spliceosome activation, and show that
mutations in the FHA domain, including the neurodevelopmental disorder-linked E366G variant,
impair this interaction, resulting in defects in splicing and cellular proliferation. Overall, our
findings define the roles of CDK11 kinase activity and the phosphorylated form of SF3B1 during
spliceosome activation and in the catalytically active spliceosome.

---

## Results

OTS964 blocks the spliceosome in a B-Bact intermediate with integrated NTR and unbound NTC.
Previously, we showed that CDK11 inhibition by OTS964 blocks spliceosome during B to Bact
transition, in a B-like intermediate 8. To define a CDK11-dependent rate-limiting step in
spliceosome activation, we decided to determine the precise protein composition of spliceosomes
blocked by OTS964 in cells. We took advantage of the fact that most pre-mRNA splicing occurs
co-transcriptionally and that spliceosomes are tightly associated with chromatin during this process
8,27,56-58. Splicing inhibitors cause the accumulation of stalled spliceosome intermediates on
chromatin, enabling their isolation and characterization directly from living cells 8,59. We treated
HCT116 cells with either DMSO (control) or 50 nM OTS964, isolated chromatin fractions, and
digested them with micrococcal nuclease (MNase) 8,59,60. The released spliceosome complexes
were immunoprecipitated with SF3B1 antibody, and the composition of SF3B1-associated
complexes was determined by mass spectrometry (Fig. 1a). Since SF3B1 is a core component of
the spliceosome (Fig. 1b), the analyses of SF3B1-associated proteins reflect the composition of a
spliceosome intermediate.

In DMSO-treated cells, approximately 30% of SF3B1-associated proteins were classified as RNA
splicing factors (GO biological process: RNA splicing) (Supplementary Data 1, sheet “IP SF3B1
(Chromatin) all data”). CDK11 inhibition significantly altered the association of 78 splicing factors
with SF3B1, with 52 proteins decreased and 26 increased in abundance (-0.5 > log2FC > 0.5, Padj
<0.05) (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Data 1, sheet “IP SF3B1 (Chromatin) all data”). Since our
previous work identified a critical role for CDK11 in the B to Bact transition 8, we followed changes
in snRNP and non-snRNP complexes involved in this transition 12. As expected, the levels of U2
snRNP and SF3B1 remained unchanged after OTS964 treatment (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Data
1, sheet “IP SF3B1 (Chromatin) splicing”). In contrast, the components of B intermediate-
associated complexes, namely U5 and U4/U6 snRNPs and B-specific proteins, increased in
abundance (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Data 1, sheet “IP SF3B1 (Chromatin) splicing”), consistent
with their accumulation upstream of a blocked transition during spliceosome activation 8. Protein
complexes that are normally recruited during spliceosome activation, such as RES, NTC and IBC,
were significantly reduced, with the notable exception of NTR, which remained unchanged,
suggesting that it was already integrated into the spliceosome. This result suggests that OTS964
arrests spliceosome progression during activation in a previously uncharacterized intermediate.

To validate this result by a method that omits the immunoprecipitation step, we isolated soluble
and chromatin fractions from cells and quantified protein levels as proxies for the presence of their
respective spliceosome complexes 8,59 (Supplementary Fig. 1a). After CDK11 inhibition, the
chromatin abundance of proteins associated with E (U2AF65), and A (RBM17) intermediates as
well as the U4/U6 snRNP (NHP2L1) complex remained equal. Meanwhile, the levels of U5
snRNP (EFTUD2, PRPF4, TXNL4A) and B-specific proteins (SMU1, IK, WBP4 and MFAP1) 
increased, and the amount of NTR (SNW1, RBM22, BUD31) complex remained unchanged
(Supplementary Fig. 1a). In contrast, proteins from RES (SNIP1, BUD13, RBMX2), NTC
(CDC5L, PRPF19), IBC (AQR) and exon-junction (EJC) (RBM8A) complexes exhibited
decreased chromatin association (Supplementary Fig. 1a). The optimal fractionation of
chromatin and effect of treatment with OTS964 were verified by histone H2A and SF3B1
phosphorylation, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1a).

This result suggests that OTS964 arrests spliceosome progression during activation in an
intermediate with integrated NTR complex, and NTC complex still not associated. We refer to this
intermediate as BOTS964.

P-SF3B1 is enriched at U6 snRNA ISL in the activated spliceosome.
The N-terminal region of SF3B1 is a large IDR containing multiple phosphorylatable Thr/Pro
repeats 8,20. As for most other IDRs of core spliceosome factors that are not resolved in cryo-EM
structures, the functional roles of the P-SF3B1 in the activated and catalytically active
spliceosomes remain unknown. Here we applied UV crosslinking and an immunoprecipitation
(iCLIP), a method that identifies direct protein-RNA interactions at single nucleotide resolution
61,62 to investigate the interaction of P-SF3B1 with U6 snRNA 8, a component of catalytically
active U2/U6 snRNA structure 63-66.

P-SF3B1 was immunoprecipitated from HCT116 cells, treated or untreated with OTS964. To
ensure the specificity of the P-SF3B1 iCLIP binding profiles, we used two phospho-specific
antibodies recognizing either P-Thr211 or P-Thr235 of SF3B1 8. Because iCLIP replicates
generated with the P-Thr211 and P-Thr235 antibodies correlated well, we combined the replicates
for each antibody and used them for further genome-wide analyses (Supplementary Fig. 2a).

To determine the contacts between P-SF3B1 and U6 snRNA, we analyzed crosslinking patterns of
P-Thr211 and P-Thr235 SF3B1 iCLIPs within U6 snRNA. Both datasets revealed a distinct peak
around nucleotide 66 in the ISL of U6 snRNA (Fig. 2a, b), suggesting an association of P-SF3B1
with this catalytically important RNA element of U6 snRNA formed in the activated spliceosome
12 (Fig. 2c). Previously published SF3B1 iCLIP data 8 showed a detectable peak at the same
position in the U6 ISL, which was insensitive to OTS964 treatment (Fig. 2d). In contrast, OTS964
treatment reduced contacts between P-SF3B1 and the ISL U6 two- to three-fold relative to total
SF3B1 at this specific position (Fig. 2a, b, d), providing further evidence for the specificity of P-
SF3B1 association with this U6 snRNA element.

As expected, neither P-SF3B1 nor total SF3B1 crosslinked to U1 snRNA which binds to 5´ splice
sites during early stages of spliceosome assembly (Supplementary Fig. 2b). By contrast, U2
snRNA, another component of the catalytically active U2/U6 snRNA spliceosome structure, was
bound predominantly by total SF3B1 and to lesser extent by P-SF3B1 (Supplementary Fig. 2c)8.

P-SF3B1 interacts with SNIP1 protein
To identify proteins that preferentially associate with P-SF3B1 in the spliceosome, we performed
a pull-down assay followed by mass spectrometry (Fig. 3a). We expressed and purified the GST-
tagged N-terminus of SF3B1 (residues 1-463) from E. coli, and phosphorylated it in vitro using
flag-tagged CDK11 purified from HEK293 cells. A non-phosphorylated version of the protein was
used as a control. GST-SF3B1 proteins were immobilized on glutathione resin and incubated with
soluble nuclear lysate from HCT116 cells. To minimize unspecific interactions with pre-assembled
spliceosome complexes, we removed the chromatin fraction and used soluble nuclear lysate treated
with RNase A to further promote the release of proteins from various RNA-dependent
subcomplexes of the spliceosome. After stringent washes, SF3B1-interacting proteins were
identified by mass spectrometry (Fig. 3a).

A comparison of proteins enriched (-1 > log2FC > 1, Padj <0.05) with phosphorylated or
unphosphorylated SF3B1 identified 8 and 26 interactors, respectively (Fig. 3b, Supplementary
Data 2). As expected, known ULM-binding proteins U2AF65 and PUF60 were detected, and
RBM39 and RBM17 31,33,34,36 were also enriched on unphosphorylated SF3B1, albeit below the
statistical significance threshold (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Data 2). These proteins are associated
with the A spliceosome intermediate in which SF3B1 remains unphosphorylated (Fig. 1b) 20,
validating the assay´s biological relevance. Among proteins preferentially associated with P-
SF3B1 was identified NIPP1, a PP1 adaptor protein that interacts with P-SF3B1 via its FHA
domain 67,68 and SNIP1, another FHA domain-containing protein and component of the RES
complex 39-41 (Fig. 3b). The presence of CDK11 and components of its complex, CCNL1/L2 and
SAP30BP 69,70, is a consequence of P-SF3B1 sample preparation (Fig. 3a, b). To validate these
interactions, we performed GST pull-down assays using (P)-SF3B1 and analyzed bound proteins
by western blotting. U2AF65 and RBM17 preferentially bound unphosphorylated SF3B1
(Supplementary Fig. 3a) and SNIP1 preferred the phosphorylated one (Fig. 3c). Notably, CDK11
remained associated with P-SF3B1 even after multiple washes, in line with the proteomics results
(Fig. 3c). Since SNIP1 contains a P-Thr binding FHA domain and is recruited to the spliceosome
during its activation (B to Bact), we focused on its functional characterization.

Acute SNIP1 depletion leads to a widespread splicing defect
To investigate the role of SNIP1 in pre-mRNA splicing and spliceosome assembly, we tagged the
endogenous SNIP1 with an inducible-degron (dTAG) system 71. dTAG facilitates the acute and
often near-complete depletion of a protein of interest, allowing for the examination of its primary
function in dynamic processes such as splicing 8,72,73. We introduced a cassette encoding a
hemagglutinin (HA) tag and the FKBP12F36V degron into both alleles of the SNIP1 gene by
CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing in HCT116 cells (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Accurate and
homozygous integration into genomic DNA was verified by sequencing (Supplementary Fig.
4b). Comparative western blot analysis of cell lysates from HCT116 and HCT116 dTAG SNIP1
cells confirmed the absence of the wild-type and the appropriate size of the tagged SNIP1 in the
edited cell line (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Upon addition of the small molecule inducer dTAG-v1,
SNIP1 was depleted specifically in the dTAG-tagged cell line, with > 90% degradation observed
within 2 h of the treatment (Supplementary Fig. 4c).

To assess how acute SNIP1 depletion impacts pre-mRNA splicing, we performed total RNA-seq
on nuclear extracts from HCT116 dTAG SNIP1 cells treated with either 500 nM dTAG-v1 or the
DMSO control for 4 h. Visual inspection of individual genes showed widespread intron retention
in transcripts from cells treated with dTAG-v1 (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 4d). For global
splicing analyses, we only considered the 6222 major isoforms of protein-coding genes with a
prevalence higher than 70%, no overlap with other genes, and with read counts per kilobase (RPK)
higher than 50, as previously described 8,73. The splicing ratio was calculated separately for 5´SS
and 3´SS by dividing the number of spliced reads by the total number of spliced and unspliced
reads crossing the respective SS. We observed significant (Wilcoxon signed rank test; p<2.2.10-
16) accumulations of unspliced reads when all the introns were considered (Fig. 4b) and also when
first, middle, and last introns were analyzed separately (Supplementary Fig. 4e). To rigorously
compare the effects of CDK11 inhibition and SNIP1 loss on splicing we compared fold changes
of intron ratios between OTS964- and DMSO-treated HCT116 cells from our previous study 8 and
between dTAG-induced SNIP1 depletion and DMSO control in dTAG SNIP1 HCT116 cells
across 12727 protein-coding genes. Intron ratios per gene were calculated as the ratio between the
total number of intronic and exonic reads for each gene as described previously 8. Only genes for
which intron ratios varied by less than two-fold between replicates in each condition were
included. This analysis revealed a strong correlation between CDK11 inhibition and SNIP1
depletion (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.79) providing evidence that CDK11 and SNIP1
affect splicing in a similar manner (Fig. 4c).

Highly similar splicing defects, observed both globally (Fig. 4b, c, Supplementary Fig. 4e) and
in individual transcripts (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 4d) after SNIP1 depletion and CDK11
inhibition 8, strongly suggest that both proteins act in the same step of spliceosome regulation. To
determine the composition of a spliceosome, intermediate after acute SNIP1 depletion and
compare it to BOTS964, we isolated chromatin fractions as in Supplementary Fig. 1a.
Immunoblotting analyses of chromatin-bound spliceosome complexes after acute SNIP1 depletion
revealed reduced levels of RES components (BUD13 and RBMX2), indicating the failure to recruit
the RES complex during the transition from B to Bact (Fig. 4d). Notably, while some subunits of
spliceosome complexes normally recruited during its activation (e.g. NTR, NTC, IBC) were still
incorporated (e.g. SNW1, RBM22, PRPF19, AQR), the others were decreased (e.g. BCAS2,
CDC5L, CWC22). Components recruited at or after the Bact stage, such as those from the EJC, C
and C* 12 complexes, were reduced or absent (Fig. 4d). The optimal fractionation of chromatin
and SNIP1 depletion were verified by using histone H4 and SNIP1 antibodies, respectively (Fig.
4d).

In summary, our results demonstrate that SNIP1 is essential for the proper recruitment of the RES
complex, and its depletion results in the accumulation of a mis-assembled, likely dead-end
spliceosome intermediate leading to widespread splicing defects.

Acute SNIP1 depletion induces OTS964-sensitive SF3B1 hyperphosphorylation
While analyzing the composition of chromatin-associated spliceosomes after either CDK11
inhibition or SNIP1 depletion, we observed an increase in U5 snRNP and B-specific proteins in
both conditions (Supplementary Fig. 1a and Fig. 4d). We interpret this accumulation as a
consequence of spliceosome stalling at the B to Bact transition. However, these perturbations had
the opposite effects on SF3B1 phosphorylation: while CDK11 inhibition diminished
phosphorylation 8 (Supplementary Fig. 1a), SNIP1 depletion caused a marked increase (Fig. 4d,
Supplementary Fig. 4c). We interpret this increase as a rapid compensatory response to the
absence of SNIP1, indicating that SF3B1 phosphorylation is a prerequisite for proper SNIP1
recruitment. An alternative explanation for the SF3B1 hyperphosphorylation is a “spliceosome
cycle arrest” with SF3B1 dephosphorylation by phosphatases being blocked while CDK11 activity
remains high. Altogether, these results are consistent with CDK11 acting as a primary kinase for
SF3B1 phosphorylation 8, and suggest that P-SF3B1 is required for the efficient integration of
SNIP1 and the RES complex to the spliceosome during its activation. To directly determine
whether this hyperphosphorylation is CDK11-dependent, we first depleted SNIP1 to induce
SF3B1 phosphorylation and subsequently treated cells with OTS964 (Fig. 5a, b, c,
Supplementary Fig. 5a). Inhibition of CDK11 for 30 min fully abrogated the phosphorylation of
SF3B1 as well as phosphorylation of Thr806 in SPT5, a recently identified CDK11 substrate 74. In
contrast, phosphorylation of the RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) C-terminal domain (CTD) on
serine 2, 5 and 7 (Ser2, Ser5 and Ser7) were reduced gradually and less specifically, as expected
upon constitutive splicing inhibition 8,73 (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 5a).

Given that previous studies have implicated transcriptional CDKs (e.g., CDK7, CDK9,
CDK12/13) in SF3B1 phosphorylation 75-79, we compared the effects of their inhibition with
OTS964. Treatment with the CDK9 inhibitor NVP-2 80, CDK12/13 inhibitor THZ531 81 or CDK7
inhibitor SY-351 75 for 30 min did not reduce P-SF3B1 levels (Fig. 5a, c, Supplementary Fig.
5a). Only a modest decrease in SF3B1 phosphorylation was observed after 1 h of CDK9 and CDK7
inhibition, whereas longer treatments (≥ 2 h) led to a substantial reduction in P-SF3B1 levels for
all inhibitors (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 5a). The decrease in SF3B1 phosphorylation observed
after longer inhibition (≥ 1 h) can be attributed to roles of these kinases in transcription, a process
upstream of splicing 8,20,72, and, in the case of CDK7 to its recently described role in CDK11
activation 75,82,83. Effective inhibition of CDK7, CDK9 and CDK12 was confirmed by the
expected changes in RNAPII CTD and SPT5 phosphorylation. Specifically, phosphorylation of
Ser5 and Ser7 in the CTD was reduced upon CDK7 inhibition 84-86; phosphorylation of Thr806 in
SPT5 and also in the CTD of RNAPII were decreased after CDK9 inhibition 80,87,88, and modest
changes in phosphorylation of Ser2 and Ser7 were detected upon longer (≥ 1 h) CDK12/13
inhibition 78,81,89-95 (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 5a). In summary, our data demonstrate that
SF3B1 hyperphosphorylation induced by SNIP1 depletion is specifically mediated by CDK11.

Two P-Thrs in SF3B1 are required for interaction with SNIP1´s FHA domain
Given that SNIP1 harbors a candidate P-Thr-binding FHA domain at its C-terminus, we tested
whether this domain is necessary for interaction with P-SF3B1 (Fig. 6a). We used in vitro binding
assays (Fig. 3a) and incubated GST-tagged (P)-SF3B1 (1-463) with his-tagged wild-type or FHA-
deletion mutant (del FHA) SNIP1 proteins expressed in E. coli (Fig. 6a). As expected, wild-type
SNIP1 associated with P-SF3B1, while deletion of the FHA domain abolished this binding
(Supplementary Fig. 6a), confirming the essential role of the FHA domain in the interaction.

FHA domains typically consist of eleven ß-strands (ß1- ß11) interspaced with six loop regions
(L1-L6), and recognize a single P-Thr via residues on apical surfaces of the loops 44,45. We used
AlphaFold 3 (AF3) 96 to model the interaction between the SNIP1 FHA domain (amino acids 259-
371) (Fig. 6b) and P-SF3B1 (amino acids 142-436). The model predicted that the SNIP1 FHA
domain interacts with two P-Thr residues in P-SF3B1, P-Thr358 and P-Thr369. The P-Thr358 is
in close proximity to SNIP1 K301 in loop L3 and P-Thr369 interacts with SNIP1 K265 in loop L1
and R365 in loop L6 (Fig. 6c).

To determine the relevance of these amino acid residues for the interaction, we generated SNIP1
mutants K265G, K301G and R365G and tested their binding to P-SF3B1 in an in vitro binding
assay (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Both K265G and K301G mutations abolished the binding, and
R365G mutation reduced binding by approximately 3-fold (Supplementary Fig. 6b). SF3B1
contains 28 Thr/Pro repeats (Supplementary Fig. 6c) that can be phosphorylated 8,20, so we next
asked whether P-Thr358 and P-Thr369 are essential for SNIP1 binding or whether they can be
substituted by the remaining P-Thr. Therefore, we mutated these two amino acids to alanine
(Thr358A and Thr369A) in the GST-SF3B1 and tested their binding to wild-type SNIP1 in an in
vitro binding assay. Since the binding of SNIP1 to the wild-type and mutated (Thr358A and
Thr369A) SF3B1 proteins remained equal, this indicates that the other P-Thr residues in SF3B1
can compensate for the loss of P-Thr358 and P-Thr369 (Supplementary Fig. 6d). These findings
suggest that the SNIP1 FHA domain recognizes multiple P-Thr residues in SF3B1, with flexibility
in which sites are utilized.

Since cryo-EM structures of the activated spliceosome (Bact) containing P-SF3B1 and RES
complex were published 13,16 we wanted to determine whether association of P-SF3B1 with FHA
domain of SNIP1 can be visualized in these structures. Close examination of the Bact complexes
(PDB: 8I0R 16 and PDB: 5Z57 13) identified a contact point between SF3B1 and SNIP1 and non-
interpreted density in the loops of the FHA domain of SNIP1 (Fig. 6d). An AF3 model of SNIP1
FHA in complex with SF3B1-derived phospho-peptide motif (P)ThrPro[X] (P)ThrPro from the
repetitive sequence of 28 Thr/Pro (Supplementary Fig. 6c) demonstrated that the predicted motif
containing two P-Thr fits exactly to the region of the unassigned cryo-EM density (CCC=0.85 at
4 Å map resolution for the AF3 prediction of SNIP1 FHA domain in complex with the SF3B1
phospho-peptide) (Fig. 6e). This observation independently validates our in vitro mutational
analysis of SNIP1-loop mutants (K265G, K301G and R365G) and supports the findings that the
FHA domain of SNIP1 binds two P-Thr in P-SF3B1 to guide the recruitment and/or anchoring of
the RES complex during the spliceosome activation.

Neurodevelopmental disorder-associated SNIP1 mutation E366G reduces binding to P-SF3B1
A homozygous SNIP1 mutation (E366G) found in ~ 35 individuals from the Amish population
has been identified as the genetic cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by
hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures (NEDHCS) 47,48. However, the molecular basis
of this mutation´s effect remains unclear. As E366 is adjacent to R365 in loop L6 of the FHA
domain, a region critical for P-Thr recognition, we hypothesized that the E366G mutant could
impair SNIP1 binding to P-SF3B1. To test this, we compared the interactions of wild-type, E366G
and R365G SNIP1 proteins with P-SF3B1 in in vitro binding assays (Supplementary Fig. 6e).

The E366G mutant exhibited an approximately 3-fold reduced binding, similar to the R365G
mutation (Supplementary Fig. 6e). Close inspection of our SNIP1-P-SF3B1 interaction model
also indicates that E366 is in close proximity to the binding interface and its mutation to glycine
(E366G) induces most likely local conformational changes in the FHA domain leading to
suboptimal P-SF3B1 binding (Fig. 6e). Altogether, these findings strongly suggest that impaired
SNIP1-P-SF3B1 interaction is the likely molecular defect underlying NEDHCS.

SNIP1 mutations in the FHA domain affect cell viability and pre-mRNA splicing
To determine whether mutations in the SNIP1 FHA domain affect incorporation of SNIP1 into the
activated spliceosome, we expressed flag-tagged SNIP1 (F-SNIP1) WT, single mutants K265G,
K301G, R365G, E366G, and the double mutant K265G/K301G in cells and compared their
association with components of the activated spliceosome (Fig. 7a, b, Supplementary Fig. 7a).
Immunoprecipitation of endogenous BUD13, a component of the RES complex, revealed
interactions with P-SF3B1 and CWC22, but not with U1-70K and U2AF65, which associate with
the spliceosome at stages preceding activation 17 (Fig. 7a, b, Supplementary Fig. 7a). These
results indicate full integration of BUD13 into the activated spliceosome. Notably, BUD13
immunoprecipitated WT F-SNIP1 more efficiently than the F-SNIP1 mutants, indicating a reduced
ability of the mutants to associate with the activated spliceosome (Fig. 7a, b, Supplementary Fig.
7a). Because substitution with glycine (G) may disrupt the FHA domain conformation, we
additionally generated alanine (A) substitutions (K265A, K301A, E365A, and K265A/K301A).
These variants also showed reduced associations with the spliceosome in BUD13
immunoprecipitates compared with WT F-SNIP1 (Supplementary Fig. 7a), confirming the
importance of residues K265, K301, and E365 for mediating interaction with P-SF3B1 in cells.
Consistent with these findings, immunoprecipitation of F-SNIP1 E366G, K265G, and double
mutant K265G/K301G revealed moderate (for E366G) and severe (for K265G and
K265G/K301G) reductions in association with components of the activated spliceosome (P-
SF3B1, CWC22, RBM22 and BUD13) (Supplementary Fig. 7b, c).

To assess the physiological importance of these FHA domain residues for cell viability and pre-
mRNA splicing, we stably integrated F-SNIP1 constructs encoding WT or mutant SNIP1 into the
FRT/TO integration site of the HCT116 dTAG SNIP1 cell line. Immunoblot analysis showed that
F-SNIP1 K265G, E366G and double K265G/K301G mutants were expressed at levels comparable
to WT F-SNIP1 (Supplementary Fig. 7d, e); therefore, subsequent analyses were performed in
these cell lines.

Cells were treated with dTAG-v1 or DMSO, and cell viability was assessed either indirectly, by
measuring metabolic activity of mitochondrial dehydrogenases by WST assay (Fig. 7c), or directly
by crystal violet staining (Fig. 7d). In the absence of ectopic F-SNIP1 expression, cells were not
viable, consistent with the essential role of SNIP1 in constitutive splicing. Expression of WT F-
SNIP1 fully rescued both metabolic activity and cellular proliferation. In contrast, the K265G and
the double K265G/K301G mutants severely impaired metabolic activity and cell viability, whereas
the patient-derived E366G mutation caused only a moderate reduction of both (Fig. 7c, d).

We next examined whether these metabolic and viability phenotypes reflected defects in pre-
mRNA splicing (Fig. 7e, f, Supplementary Fig. 7f). Splicing of endogenous RIOK3, ARRDC1,
and CCNL1 transcripts was analyzed by RT-PCR following dTAG-v1 treatment. Accumulation of
unspliced transcripts was evident within 2 h of SNIP1 depletion in HCT116 dTAG-SNIP1 cells
(Fig. 7e, f). This splicing defect was partially rescued by expression of WT F-SNIP1, confirming
that the phenotype was specific to SNIP1 depletion (Fig. 7e, f). In contrast, expression of F-SNIP1
K265G, E366G, or the double K265G/K301G mutant failed to rescue, or rescued less efficiently,
the splicing defects compared with WT F-SNIP1 (Fig. 7e, f). Notably, the double K265G/K301G
mutant consistently showed a more severe defect than the patient-derived E366G mutation (Fig.
7e). These differences were further supported by quantitative PCR analysis of splicing of long
introns in the CCNL1 and SFSWAP genes (Supplementary Fig. 7f), indicating that the observed
splicing defects are general and not dependent on intron length. Taken together, these results
demonstrate that FHA domain residues mediating interaction with P-SF3B1 are essential for
efficient pre-mRNA splicing and cell viability.

## Methods

Antibodies, Primers, Plasmids and Reagents
Lists of antibodies, primers, plasmids and reagents used in the study are provided in
Supplementary Data 3.

Cell culture
HEK293 Flp-in cell line (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R75007), human colorectal HCT116 cell line
(ATCC) and its variant HCT116 Flp-in cell line (a gift from B. G. Wouters), were maintained in
DMEM/high-glucose medium supplemented with L-glutamine, sodium pyruvate and 5% FBS at
37 °C and 5% CO . The cell lines were negatively tested for mycoplasma contamination with
2
MycoStrip Mycoplasma Detection Kit (InvivoGen, rep-mys-20).

To prepare HCT116 Flp-in cell line with inducible degradation of SNIP1 protein, we used
CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing with the PITCh system 119, and proceeded according to the
published protocol 120. sgRNA (CAGCCAAAATCACAGAATGA) targeting N-terminus of
SNIP1 gene was cloned into pX330-BbsI-PITCh (addgene #127875) 121 and microhomology arms
surrounding CRISPR-Cas9 cleavage site (each 20bp long) were introduced into donor plasmid
pCRIS-PITChv2-Puro-dTAG (addgene #91793) 71.

HCT116 Flp-in cells (seeded in 10 cm plates, 30% confluency) were co-transfected with 9 μg of
donor plasmid and 3 μg of sgRNA-Cas9 plasmid, and 24 μl Turbofect (Thermo Scientific, R0533)
in 2 ml Opti-MEM (Thermo Scientific, 11058-021). Medium was changed 2 h post-transfection.
Cells were transferred to 15 cm plates two days post-transfection and resistant colonies were
selected with 0.3 µg/ml puromycin (Merck, P8833) for at least 2 weeks. Individual colonies were
expanded in 12 well plates, genomic DNA was extracted with PureLink Genomic DNA Mini Kit
(Thermo Scientific, K182002), as well as protein lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer (50 mM
Tris-Cl, pH 8, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS,
supplemented with protease inhibitors, Sigma, P8340). Clones with homozygous integration of the
dTAG cassette at the SNIP1 locus were validated by Sanger sequencing and immunoblotting.

We selected clone (#28) with proper integration of dTAG cassette (named as HCT116 dTAG
SNIP1) for further experiments and verified rapid degradation of SNIP1 protein by treating the
cells with 500 nM dTAGv-1 (MedChemExpress, HY-145514).

We modified HCT116 dTAG SNIP1 cells by stable integration of flag-tagged SNIP1 (F-SNIP1)
gene into flp-in site. We prepared five derivative cell lines expressing different F-SNIP1 mutants
(WT, K265G, K265G&K301G and E366G). We verified both ectopic integration of F-SNIP1
variants by Sanger sequencing of their genomic DNA and F-SNIP1 expression by western blotting
with SNIP1 antibody (after induction with 1μg/ml doxycycline for 24 h).

Cell proliferation assays
All clones were seeded into four 96-well plate (400 cells / well; 6 wells per clone per plate) and
expression of F-SNIP1 variants was induced with doxycycline (1 mg/1 ml of media). The next day
dTAG-v1 (500 nM final concentration) or DMSO (solvent) were added and cells were cultured for
another 24, 48 and 72 hours, respectively. Each day cell growth was measured by WST assay
(ab65473, Abcam).

For crystal violet staining individual clones were seeded into 100 mm dishes (4 x 105 cells / dish) and
expression of F-SNIP1 variants was induced with doxycycline (1 mg/1 ml of media). The next
day dTAG-v1 (500 nM final concentration) or DMSO (solvent) were added and cells were cultured for
another 72 hours. Media was replaced every day and after three days the cells were fixed with
methanol: acetic acid (3:1) and stained with crystal violet.

Chromatin isolation and mass spectrometry analyses of SF3B1-associated proteins
Chromatin-associated protein complexes were isolated according to mNET-seq protocol 60.
Protein complexes were released from chromatin by mild MNase digestion, and finally
immunoprecipitated with endogenous antibodies. Immunoprecipitated proteins were detected by
mass spectrometry.

HCT116 cells were plated onto 15 cm plates (three plates per condition) to reach 80% confluency
at the day of experiment. Plates were washed twice with ice-cold PBS, scraped, pelleted 250 g at
4°C for 3 min and treated on ice for 5 min with 4 ml of ice-cold HLB+N buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl
(pH 7.5), 10 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM MgCl , 0.5% NP-40, 1x phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Sigma,
2
P0044) and 1x protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma, P8340)). The cell pellet was underlaid with 1
ml of ice-cold HLB+NS (10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 10 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM MgCl , 0.5% NP-40,
2
10% sucrose, 1x phosphatase inhibitor cocktail and 1x protease inhibitor cocktail). Nuclei were
pelleted by centrifugation (420 g, 4 °C for 5 min) and supernatant was discarded. Pellets were
resuspended by vortexing in 100 μl NUN1 buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCL (pH = 7.5), 75 mM
NaCl, 0.5 mM EGTA, 50 % glycerol, 1x protease and 1x phosphatase inhibitors. Chromatin was
extracted by addition of 1 ml of NUN2 buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH = 7.6), 7.5 mM
MgCl , 0.2 mM EGTA, 300 mM NaCl, 1 M urea and 1 % NP-40, 1x protease and 1x phosphatase
2
inhibitors and rotated at 4°C for 10 min. After centrifugation (1600 g, 4°C for 5 min), supernatant
was completely removed. Chromatin pellet was washed once with 1 ml of MNase buffer, digested
with MNase at 37 °C for 6 min at 1400 rpm. MNase was inactivated by EGTA (20 mM final
concentration). After centrifugation (1600 g, 4°C for 5 min), supernatant was diluted by two
volumes of NET-2 buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH=7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% NP-40, 1x protease
and 1x phosphatase inhibitors) and pre-cleared by protein G Dynabeads at 4 °C for 1 h.
Immunoprecipitation was performed with SF3B1 antibody (MBL, MB-221-3, 5 μl).

Immunoprecipitated samples were washed four times with 1 ml of NET-2 buffer and stored in 10
mM Tris-HCl (pH=8.1) at -80 °C.

Beads-bound protein complexes were mixed with 2 % SDS solution and heated to 50 ℃ for 20 min
following protein reduction using 100 mM DITT at 95 ℃ for 15 min. Resulting protein solutions
were subjected to filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) as described elsewhere 122 covering
proteins alkylation (100 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for 20 min in dark at laboratory temperature)
and proteins digestion using 0.75 μg of trypsin (sequencing grade; Promega). Peptides were then
cleaned by liquid-liquid extraction (3 iterations) using water saturated ethyl acetate 123. Cleaned
FASP eluates were evaporated completely in SpeedVac concentrator (Thermo Fisher Scientific)
and transferred into LC-MS vial containing PEG (final concentration 0.001%, v/v) using 25 μl of
50% acetonitrile (ACN) with 2.5% formic acid (FA) and 100 μl of ACN. SpeedVac was used for
transferred peptides concentration and ACN removal with final volume adjustment using MilliQ
water. Resulting peptide solutions were analyzed by liquid chromatography–tandem mass
spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) performed using UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system (Thermo Fisher

to Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Prior to LC
separation, tryptic digests were online concentrated and desalted using trapping column
(Acclaim™ PepMap™ 100 C18, dimensions 300 μm ID, 5 mm long, 5 μm particles, Thermo

(New Objective) ion source with sheath gas option. ABIRD (Active Background Ion Reduction
Device, ESI Source Solutions) was installed.

MS data were acquired in a data-dependent strategy (cycle time 2.5 s). Survey scan range was set
to m/z 350-2000 with the resolution of 120,000 (at m/z 200), normalized target value of 250 %
and maximum injection time of 500 ms. HCD MS/MS spectra (isolation window m/z 1.2, 30%
relative fragmentation energy) were acquired from 110 m/z with a target value of 5×104, resolution
of 15,000 (at m/z 200) and maximum injection time of 50 ms. Dynamic exclusion was enabled for
30 s.

The analysis of the mass spectrometric RAW data files was carried out using the MaxQuant
software (version 2.0.1.0) 124 using default settings unless otherwise noted. MS/MS ion searches
were done against modified cRAP database (based on http://www.thegpm.org/crap) containing
protein contaminants like keratin, trypsin etc., and UniProtKB protein database for Homo sapiens
(downloaded 2021-06-16, number of protein sequences: 20,600). Oxidation of methionine,
deamidation (N, Q) and acetylation (protein N-terminus) as optional modification,
carbamidomethylation (C) as a fixed modification and trypsin/P enzyme with two allowed miss
cleavages were set. Peptides and proteins with FDR threshold <0.01 and proteins having at least
one unique or razor peptide were considered only. Match between runs was set among all analyzed
samples. Protein abundance was assessed using protein intensities calculated by MaxQuant.

Reported protein intensities were further processed using the software container environment
(https://github.com/OmicsWorkflows). Processing workflow is available upon request. Briefly, it
covered: a) removal of decoy hits and contaminant protein groups, b) protein group intensities log2

Major Isoform Selection and Splicing Ratio Analysis
The primary transcript isoforms were determined following established protocols 73. RNA-
sequencing data was processed using the NF-Core pipeline 127 (Nextflow v23.04.1) from the NF-
Core consortium (v3.14, available at https://github.com/nf-core/rnaseq; archived at
https://zenodo.org/records/10471647). To identify the predominant isoform for each gene,
sequencing reads were mapped with Salmon 128 (v1.10.1) against curated UCSC RefSeq
annotations (GRCh38, downloaded July 2024). The isoform exhibiting the highest mean
transcript-per-million (TPM) value across all samples was designated as the major isoform,
provided it accounted for at least 70% of the gene’s isoform expression. Isoforms associated with
overlapping genes and those located on chromosomes X, Y, and M were excluded.

Splicing ratios were computed via an exon-centric splice junction analysis 58. Only exons from
major isoforms with an initial exon exceeding 100 base pairs were considered, while isoforms
annotated as single-exon were excluded. A window spanning ±4 base pairs around each splice
junction (2 bp in the exon and 2 bp in the intron) was defined to assess both spliced and unspliced
reads using the findOverlaps function from the GenomicRanges 129 R package (v1.56). Reads
overlapping at least 3 bp of this window were classified as unspliced, whereas reads overlapping
at least 2 bp were counted as total reads (spliced and unspliced). Spliced reads were determined
by subtracting the unspliced count from the total. The splicing ratio was calculated as the
proportion of spliced reads relative to the total, spliced and unspliced reads 73.

iCLIP Data Analysis
iCLIP sequencing data, including total, P-Thr211- and P-Thr235 SF3B1 samples, were analyzed
on the flow.bio platform (https://app.flow.bio/) using the nf-core/clipseq 130 pipeline (v1.0;
https://github.com/nf-core/clipseq/tree/1.0.0). Initial processing involved removing experimental
barcodes (iCount version 2.0.0, de-multiplex function https://github.com/tomazc/iCount),
followed by read alignment with STAR 131 against the human reference genome (hg38,
GRCh38.p13 primary assembly, GENCODE version 39), allowing up to two mismatches. Unique
molecular identifiers (UMIs) were applied to identify and eliminate PCR duplicates. Cross-linking
events were determined by identifying the nucleotide immediately preceding each uniquely
mapped sequencing read.

Genome-wide coverage tracks for combined iCLIP replicates were generated using deepTools 132,
normalized by sequencing depth and total read count, and binned per nucleotide. cDNA counts at
individual iCLIP cross-link sites were normalized to the total number of reads in each experimental
library and scaled to counts per million (CPM). Metagene density plots were generated from
normalized coverage data across all RNUs. To account for variations in region lengths between
main and pseudogene RNUs, the mode distance was used to scale the signal for each RNU class
as follows: RNU1 (116 genes, 163 nt), RNU2 (39 genes, 190 nt), RNU4 (54 genes, 140 nt), RNU5
(25 genes, 115 nt), and RNU6 (505 genes, 106 nt).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors sought to explain a requirement for SF3B1 phosphorylation by cyclin-dependent kinase 11 (CDK11) in pre-mRNA splicing, which they established in their previous work (ref. 8). Here they use mass spectrometry and iCLIP to analyze protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions, respectively, of SF3B1 in human colon cancer cells in the absence or presence of the selective CDK11 inhibitor OTS964. They uncover a novel intermediate in spliceosome assembly/ activation, designated as “BOTS964”, which is blocked after association with U4 and U6 snRNPs but prior to recruitment of the RES complex and subsequent enzyme activation. They show that the RES complex subunit SNIP1 is needed for this interaction—and to support normal splicing—by introducing a degron tag (dTAG) into SNIP1 in HCT116 cells; and that the forkhead-associated (FHA) domain of SNIP1 is necessary for phosphorylation-dependent binding to the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of SF3B1 in pulldown assays in vitro. Finally, the authors present evidence that a SNIP1-FHA mutant variant implicated in a neurodevelopmental disorder is defective in binding phosphorylated SF3B1 (P-SF3B1) in vitro. Overall, this is a well-designed and –executed study. Most of the major conclusions are well supported by the data, and will be of high interest to the readers of Nature Communications. There are, however, some deficiencies—most significantly, a missed opportunity to test effects of SNIP1-FHA mutations on splicing in living cells—that should be addressed in a revised manuscript.
Specific concerns:
1. Line 2: The title is generally a bit acronym-heavy, and in particular I’m afraid readers outside the field will not know what “RES” is. I would recommend giving them at least a clue by saying “RES complex” (minor).
2. In Figure 1c, there are a couple of extreme outliers whose association with SF3B1 drops more drastically than the others in the same complexes (NTC and IBC). What are these (they should probably be labeled)? Are they known to be more loosely associated with their respective complexes, or more labile?
3. Lines 172-173: Looking at the correlation analysis in Fig S2b, it is an overstatement to say that the iCLIP replicates for the two anti-P-SF3B1 antibodies “correlated well” (Pearson correlation coefficients for the DMSO treated samples are mostly around 0.5, whereas the OTS964-treated samples show lower correlation, presumably because of lower yield). Compare this to the strong correlations reported in ref. 8 for the total SF3B1 antibody (ED Fig. 9d).
4. Lines 186-189: I am not sure I follow the logic that leads the authors to state that the reduction of P-SF3B1 binding to the U6 internal stem-loop (ISL) “is likely an underestimate.” As I understand the normalization scheme, the OTS964-treated sample was overrepresented (in terms of cell equivalents) to account for decreased protein-RNA binding, but shouldn’t this boost both ISL and non-ISL read counts equally? It is the relative enrichment of ISL in the two conditions (DMSO vs. OTS964) that is being measured here, so I’m not really sure what is being underestimated.
5. Relatedly, I was unable to deduce from the data shown what the quantitative effect of CDK11 inhibition on U6 binding was (as opposed to the qualitative effect on sequence specificity depicted in Fig. 2). Can this be estimated based on the iCLIP data with the pan-specific anti-SF3B1 antibody?
6. ### Reviewer 3

The manuscript from Gajduskova et. al., describes the role of phosphorylation of SF3B1 (P-SF3B1) in defining a novel intermediate spliceosome B complex (called the B-OTS964), how p-SF3B1 interacts with U6 snRNA, and the role of SNIP1,a component of the RES complex in spliceosome activation. The work follows the groups recent published work that showed CDK11 phosphorylation of SF3B1 using OTS964. The study uses biochemical and genome-wide approaches for these. Use of endogenously dTAG-inserted SNIP1 for acute degradation strengthens many of the studies. A major limitation is that many of the results have already been described in more rigorous structural studies. Overall, it is unclear what is novel, and what the precise message is.
Major:
1. The proposed novel intermediate B-OTS964 is entirely based on biochemical data, which is speculated to have NTR incorporated without NTC. Authors are remiss of intermediate Bact structures reported with cryEM structures have recently been reported with the same configuration of NTR incorporation without NTC (PMID: 39068178). It is unclear why this was not included in references and clarify how the biochemical studies add or refine to this structure.
2. Similarly, the configuration of SNIP1, a component of RES has been described in other recent solved structures of Bact (PMID: 37165190). This important context is missing and the reference not included – including this help understand what is novel in the findings.
3. iCLIP showing U6 binding to SF3B1 is presented as novel although the group’s on previous publication (PMID: 36104565) touched upon this. With current known confirmations of Bact, it is not clear why this would be considered novel. Critically, iCLIP for other snRNA is missing ( one would expect strong binding to U2 and minimal interaction with U1).
4. The claim that CDK11 and SNIP1 act on the same step of spliceosome regulation (line 262) is not supported by the data. In fact analysis of splicing is restricted to global splicing changes at 5’SS and 3’SS. Biochemical analysis of splicing (denaturing gel) and global alternative splicing changes (such as rMATS or SUPPA) are missing. Furthermore, to make a claim that CDK11 and SNIP1 loss have similar effects on splicing, overlap analysis of AS changes in the two conditions should be considered. Otherwise it remains broad failure of splicing.
5. While the manuscript is heavily reliant on IP and in vitro binding assays, none of these show replicate data or quantification. The critical findings need to be shown as quantified from replicates and statistics.
6. The assertion that phenotype of E336G homozygosity is due to impaired SNIP1-SF3B1 interaction is not supported by the data presented. Interaction of the mutant with other components of RES or Bact are not shown. Nor is the impact on splicing attempted.
Minor:
1. Per structural studies, SF3B1 is not present in B*/C as suggested in the text and Figure 1. This does not affect the conclusions of the study but is important to correct.
2. iCLIP is semi quantitative given lack of input control. To make quantitiave assumptions is problematic and needs to be discussed/
3. pSer2 changes in Fig 5C appear minimal and not quantitated. As presented, it does not fully support the claim that CDK9 or 12 does not have effects similar to CDK11 on SF3B1. Longer time points and higher concentrations need to be tested with quantitation to make that claim.
4. it is unclear why some components of NTC like BCAS2 fall while others such as CDC5L are unchanged with SNIP1 loss. This needs to be discussed in the context of sequential addition of RES, NTR and NTC and available structural data. This is yet another reason to include quantification with replicates for such single blot data.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript by Gajdušková et al. reveals the role that CDK11-mediated phosphorylation of SF3B1 plays in the specific recruitment of the retention and splicing (RES) complex, which enables proficient splicing. Using the CDK11 inhibitor OTS964, the authors stabilise an intermediate spliceosomal complex, enabling them to investigate the precise function of C-terminal SF3B1 phosphorylation. They elegantly demonstrate that inhibitor treatment causes the loss and gain of critical interactors relevant for the transition from the spliceosomal B complex to the Bact complex. They specifically identify the RES components SNIP1 and BUD13 as direct interactors of the phospho-SF3B1 domain, and demonstrate that loss of SNIP1 (dTAG) or phospho-SF3B1 (OTS964) leads to impaired splicing.
Through further mutational investigations, the authors were able to determine how SNIP1 interacts with the phospho-SF3B1 domain, leading them to formulate a well-founded hypothesis regarding the relevance of an E366G mutation in SNIP1 in a neurodevelopmental context.
The quality of the data and clarity of the manuscript make this a very interesting study for splicing enthusiasts. A few additional suggestions could be considered without the need for major experiments.
- Supplementary Table 1: It would be helpful to have a table with all proteins detected in complex with SF3B1 (+/-OTS964) and not just the spliceosome-relevant ones.
- Figure 1D, Supplementary Fig 1A: How much do these complexes rely on the presence of RNA? Have the authors performed experiments with RNase treatment and thus they assume that all of these interactions are mediated by direct interaction with SF3B1 or are they rather mediated by RNA or a mix of both? The authors should comment on the usage of RNase treatment in the text, as likely many of these interactions are not direct interactors. Could the authors also include RNase treatment-based SF3B1 co-IP experiments to cross-validate their in vitro binding assay experiments?
- If indeed the recruitment of different subcomplexes is reliant on RNA and/or protein–protein interactions and the IBC complex does not appear to be direct binders of (P-)SF3B1 (Figure 3B), what is the rationale for the lack of this complex from the SF3B1-enriched chromatin fraction after OTS964 treatment? (Steric hindrance with U4 snRNP as well or loss of RES recruitment?)
- Supplementary Figure 2A: “…resulting in a weaker radioactive signal for RNA-P-SF3B1 complexes…” – Does the autoradiograph really indicate reduced RNA interaction or just reduced IP efficiency because less of the phosphorylated protein is IPed? The authors should provide a WB with their radioactive gels in order to assess IP efficiency versus reduced RNA binding. Otherwise, this statement should be revised. Statements related to understimating the effect of the CDK11 inhibitor on the phospho-SF3B1 iCLIP signal (lines 186–189): The unspecific coverage around the U6 ISL binding site appear to be similar between the libraries. Would this not mean that the general enrichment of U6 sites is similar despite differences in the iCLIP library size? Also, again one needs to ensure that this is a reflection of decreased binding and not of decreased IP efficiency.
- Figure 2A/B: The transition in the text from the BP CLIP signal to the U6 snRNA focus is not clear. Why are the authors looking at the U6 snRNA? Could the authors include the interaction surface with the U2 snRNA as this should form a complex with the branchpoint. This would be further validation of the U2 snRNP being intake. This paper might be helpful here to infer interaction sites: 10.1261/rna.065664.118
- Supplementary Figure 2F: Do the authors not find the lack of U6-binding of SFB31 (iCLIP) somewhat concerning? Should the U6 binding not be recovered in SF3B1 data as well, if this was a functionally relevant complex? How sure can the authors be that in the phospho-SF3B1 IP conditions they are only enriching P-SF3B1 protein and nothing else that is part of the complex (have the authors performed proteomics of their IPs?)? Could it be that the U6 binding peak originates from a co-precipitated component? Further experiments should be performed to show interaction of P-SF3B1 to U6. However, seeing as the authors do not go back or use this novel discovery for any further arguments, it might be sufficient to just limit the claim here a little bit.
- Given that the authors have prepared iCLIP data for P-SF3B1 and RNAseq data for the CDK11 inhibitor, could the authors generate RNA maps to visualize whether the P-SF3B1 binding is preferentially located at CDK11 inhibitor-sensitive sites (similar to 10.1261/rna.069237.118). Could the identity of the targets (GO terms might help here) somehow explain why neurons cannot deal with the SNIP1 mutation?
- Figure 4D: SNIP1 is known as a transcriptional regulator and acts as an inhibitor of the coactivators CBP and p300 and acts on TGF-beta (J. Biol. Chem. 276:46297-46304 (2001)) and NF-kB signalling. Do the authors see changes in the expression specifically of these pathways as well? Does this play a role here? Previous publications for SNIP1 should be discussed and considered here as well.
- Figure 4A/D: Given that there are cryoEM structures available, could the authors include a figure to indicate where on the structure SF3B1 and SNIP1 lie and whether they can actually directly interact in the Bact complex (10.1038/cr.2018.14).
- Figure 5B: Given that BUD13 is also a direct interactor of the phosphorylated-CTD of SF3B1 as per MS and WB, why is this protein not sufficient to assemble the RES to promote productive splicing? Can this be rationalized by looking at the structure of the whole complex or further assembly? Why do all three components need to be there? Would loss of BUD13 result in the same effects?
- Figure 5A/B: Why does loss of SNIP1 lead to CDK11-dependent hyperphosphorylation? Could the authors include some further discussion of this point?

Response: A precise quantitative effect cannot be determined without input material and, ideally, spike-in controls, which are not trivial to implement for iCLIP-seq. However, because the total SF3B1 iCLIP peak over the U6 ISL remains unchanged between DMSO- and OTS964-treated samples after normalization to read counts (Fig. 2d), we can estimate that the reduction in P-SF3B1 binding to the U6 ISL upon OTS964 treatment is approximately 2–3-fold (Fig. 2a, b). This estimate is consistent with our previously published RIP-qPCR data (doi: 10.1038/s41586-022-05204-z, Extended Data Fig. 10), which were normalized to percent of input and decrease of P-SF3B1 binding upon OTS964 is also observed.
Importantly, OTS964 treatment, as well as the use of two independent phospho-specific SF3B1 antibodies, provides an internal control for the specificity of the P-SF3B1 iCLIP signal. The reproducible P-SF3B1 crosslink patterns on U6, as well as on U1 and U2 snRNAs (now included in the manuscript as Supp. Fig. 2b, c), support the conclusion that phosphorylated SF3B1, that is present only in the activated spliceosome, can indeed contact the U6 ISL.
6. Lines 213-216: The enrichment of CDK11 and its binding partners (cyclin L, SAP30BP) in the pulldown of P-SF3B1 seems likely to be a trivial consequence of sample preparation differences, i.e., pre-treating only this sample with purified, FLAG-tagged CDK11 complexes. Concluding anything about CDK11’s relative affinities for P-SF3B1 vs. SF3B1 would require a better-controlled experiment, e.g. -/+ ATP, or the use of a catalytically dead mutant CDK11 to generate the non-phosphorylated sample. The authors should probably point this out limitation.
Response: In this experiment we did not wish to make any conclusion regarding relative affinities of the CDK11 complex for P-SF3B1 versus SF3B1 and we agree that the presence of the complex in P-SF3B1 sample is most likely a consequence of the sample preparation. We have corrected the relevant section of the text so this is clear.
7. Lines 256-258: Here is the missed opportunity. Having established the dTAG-SNIP1 system and achieving rescue of splicing defects by ectopic SNIP expression (albeit partial, likely because of low expression), I would like to have seen tests of the various mutant forms of SNIP that abolish or impair binding in vitro to P-SF3B1—K265G, K301G. R365G, E366G—for their ability to rescue.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. For technical reasons we initially had a problem to prepare flag-tagged SNIP1 (F-SNIP1) proteins (including E366G mutant) that would have similar expression levels with WT F-SNIP1. Comparable amounts of expression are important for the follow up RT(q)-PCR experiments and proper functional comparison between the SNIP1 proteins. In the revised manuscript we were have been able to prepare F-SNIP1 E366G (patient mutation), K265G and double mutant K265G, K301G cell lines, that have similar protein expression levels to the cell line carrying F-SNIP1 WT (Supp. Fig.7 d, e). We performed comparison of splicing by RT-PCR (on agarose gel) and by qPCR on several selected genes and can now observe defect in splicing in all the SNIP1 mutants when compared to F-SNIP1 WT. The data are now presented in Fig. 7e, f and Supp. Fig. 7f.
Additionally, we performed proliferation assays with these SNIP1 cell lines after depletion of dTAG-SNIP1 and the mutations affected cellular proliferation correspondingly to their splicing defects. Specifically, patient mutation SNIP1 E366G slowed but did not stop the cellular proliferation, while the other SNIP1 mutations stopped the cellular proliferation more severely. These data are now included in the Fig. 7c, d and support the hypothesis that the mutations affect core splicing and correspondingly also the cellular proliferation.
8. Relatedly, Gly substitutions are notoriously disruptive of protein conformation; is there a rationale behind changing basic residues to Gly rather than, say, Ala (or acidic residues)?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We originally mutated K301, R365 and K265 to Gly, the same residue present in patients (E366G). As suggested we performed mutation of these residues to Ala and tested incorporation of these SNIP1 proteins to the spliceosome by transient transfection in cells. All tested mutations (i.e. K301A, R365A, K265A and K265A K301A) were less efficiently incorporated to the spliceosome when compared to WT F-SNIP1. This experiment suggests that the observed phenotypes are not just effect of replacement of the tested residues with potentially disruptive Gly mutations on the FHA structure of SNIP1. The results of these experiments are included now in the Supp Fig. 7a.
9. Lines 291-298 and Fig. 5c: The intent here was to determine the specificity (or exclusivity) of SF3B1 as a CDK11 substrate, given previous reports that other transcriptional CDKs phosphorylate this protein; the conclusion that an OTS964-sensitive kinase is required for the bulk of SF3B1 phosphorylation in cells is probably correct, but the analysis is both incomplete and flawed. Among the flaws or omissions: 1) although CDK7 is named as a candidate SF3B1 kinase (based on ref. 70), no CDK7-selective inhibitor is tested; 2) the CDK9 inhibitor NVP-2 is tested at a very low dose (30 nM) and with a substrate (RNAPII CTD) that is probably not the best (SPT5 is more sensitive and specific: see, for example: doi: 10.1038/s41467-020-18173-6); 3) even so, NVP-2 treatment does decrease the upshifted (i.e., phosphorylated) SF3B1 detected with the pan-specific antibody at the 3-hour time point, but this is not commented upon; 4) the “slightly increased” phospho-Ser2 signal seen after treatment with the CDK12/13 inhibitor THZ531 does not agree with at least one previous study using this compound, which showed a decrease (doi: 10.1038/nchembio.2166); and 5) none of the effects are quantified.
Response: We included all these suggestions (and suggestions of the reviewer 3) and in the new version of the Fig. 5c and new Supp. Fig. 5a we show effects of 1) CDK7 inhibition with inhibitor SY-351, 2) use increased concentration of NVP-2 inhibitor (100 nM) and include SPT5 as an additional control substrate and 3) comment on the results in the Result section. Additionally, 4) we cite papers where CDK12 was inhibited (either by selective inhibition of its analog-sensitive version or THZ531) and comment on inhibition by THZ531 in the context of the CDK12/CDK13 literature and 5) given the high number of samples, we chose to present two replicates in the paper and an additional replicate 3 in Raw Data File, instead of quantification.
Of note, CDK7 or CDK9 inhibition do not result in changes in vitro splicing assays using an RNA reporter and nuclear extract (see doi: 10.1093/nar/gkaf1343; Supp. Fig. 6e and doi: 10.1038/s41586-022-05204-z; Extended Data Fig. 7h). This is in contrast to CDK11 inhibition by OTS964 that affects splicing in vitro (see doi: 10.1038/s41586-022-05204-z; Fig. 3a, b). This provides an additional strong argument that the inhibition of CDK7 and CDK9 do not affect splicing (and SF3B1 phosphorylation) directly, but just indirectly.
10. Lines 380-382 and Fig. 7b: In both the cartoon model and the indicated text, the authors seem to imply that the phosphorylated residues of the SF3B1 IDR are interacting directly with the ISL of U6 snRNA, but, besides being electrostatically unfavorable (as the authors seem to acknowledge), this is not actually supported by any data. What the iCLIP data with the phospho-specific antibodies show is that phosphorylation confers specificity on SF3B1 for the ISL, but this is as likely (or more likely) to be due to a conformational change in the protein upon phosphorylation. For one thing, for this method to work, the antibody needs access to the phosphorylated residues but can’t be disrupting the interaction with RNA. The authors should clarify this in the text and modify Fig. 7b to avoid confusion about this point or inaccuracy in their model.
Response: iCLIP-seq relies on UV crosslinking, which captures only direct RNA–protein contacts before immunoprecipitation under stringent conditions (doi: 10.1016/j.ymeth.2013.10.011). Thus, antibody binding should not interfere with crosslinked RNA-protein interaction. However, we agree that the P-SF3B1 contacts detected on U6 snRNA in the iCLIP data could arise not only from direct interaction of the phosphorylated residues themselves, but also—as the reviewer notes—from phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes within SF3B1 or the spliceosome. Notably, electrostatically unfavorable “interaction” between P-SF3B1 peptides and an RNA was also independently detected in reference 28 (doi: 10.1016/j.molcel.2022.03.024).
OTS964 treatment affects both, SF3B1 phosphorylation status (thereby reducing recovery with phospho-specific antibodies) and the conformational state of the SF3B1 N-terminus. These two effects cannot be separated in our current dataset. We now acknowledge this explicitly in the Discussion. In the Results section, we have already stated that “OTS964 treatment significantly weakened this interaction, underscoring the importance of both SF3B1 phosphorylation and RNA structure formation in Bact assembly,”. Additionally, we have expanded the Discussion, adjusted the wording throughout the manuscript and text to Fig. 8 legend to clarify that the schematic model and iCLIP results do not explicitly imply that the phosphorylated residues directly bind to the U6 ISL. Instead, the figure legend has been revised to clarify the phosphorylation of SF3B1 as enabling or stabilizing the conformation that allows SF3B1 to engage the U6 ISL.
The observed relative decrease in P-SF3B1 binding to the U6 ISL with OTS964 treatment, and the consistent results obtained with two independent phospho-specific antibodies, both serve as controls confirming the specificity of the P-SF3B1 iCLIP signal. We have clarified these points in the revised result text and figure legend.

Response: This was corrected

Response: Supplemental Fig. 5 is now included.
